The Sasol Solar Challenge

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Shining a spotlight on the brilliant engineers of the Sasol Solar Challenge

Unique Selling Point:
In an era of climate change and the urgency to harness renewable energy forms, the Sasol Solar Challenge provides a platform for the best and brightest engineering students in the country. Every second year South Africa hosts some of the best teams from across the world, exposing our local students to an invaluable variety of experts, sponsors, technologies and innovations in a quest to build a the best solar-powered car in the world.


Summary:
The Sasol Solar Challenge is an eight-day event in which local and international solar-powered cars travel as far as they can on various roads between Pretoria and Cape Town, some covering a distance of up to 4 000 km. Taking place from 24 September to 1 October 2016 this year, Sasol Solar Challenge is aimed at promoting science, technology, engineering and mathematics among university students and the broader public by illustrating the role of these disciplines in an ingenious way. The competition also aims to promote the power of alternative energy, notably solar.




Further information:
In this story, we will focus our attention on 3 of the South African universities competing:

The North West University - This is the team featured in a previous Carte Blanche story on the World Solar Challenge in Australia. We will catch up with the team and see how they've progressed since we last saw them.

The University of Johannesburg - This is one of the oldest South African teams – having competed in almost every Solar Challenge in SA. Their car is advanced and is a top competitor. The UJ team has a young rising star called Roberto de Carvalho who designed large parts of the car without any guidance from mentors or lecturers, and much of his work has been used as is. He is now the team’s designated aerodynamicist. He’s only 25 years old.

Tshwane University of Technology - TUT’s biggest story is that they are doing this entire project on a budget of R2 million, which is an incredibly small budget for a solar car. Despite this, they believe they have a competitive vehicle, and have entered into the toughest class of the event – the Challenger class. That said, TUT has one of the best engineering departments in South Africa in terms of research and innovation outputs - and have completely redone their 2016 vehicle from scratch.

The shoot will take place over two days:

September 22 - Swartkops Raceway: This is a designated track day in which all team cars participating undergo mandatory testing that they have to pass in order to be allowed to compete in the race. All of the teams will be there and I have already secured interviews with team members from NWU, UJ & TUT. We will also have access to their pitlanes to be able to shoot their cars in detail. Whilst at Swartkops, we will also be able to meet some of the international teams taking part including favourites from the Netherlands and Japan

September 30 - 1 October - This is the final leg of the race from Swellendam to Cape Town. We will rendezvous with the race at Swellendam on the 30th, camp the night with the teams before they leave at 6:30AM for the final stage to Cape Town. We will shoot this final leg along with the finish at the V&A Waterfront.

The 3 SA university teams have agreed to provide R&D material of their cars in the form of video, cad design & still photos to augment the insert.

The race organisers have agreed to provide footage of the race (stage 1-7) captured by their videographer

09 October 2016 - Carte Blanche HDNikola Vrahimis01 November 2016

Press Release:


Imagine travelling from Pretoria to Cape Town and never stopping to fill the tank. Local and international participants in this year’s Sasol Solar Challenge have just spent eight days in cars that, powered only by the sun, travel as far as they can go on roads between Pretoria and Cape Town—the winners reaching over 4000 kilometres. Carte Blanche meets contenders in a race to promote the power of alternative energy.

Script:


VOICE OVER: Every morning we wake up to something we all take for granted: the rising of the sun.

Our nearest star, over 150 million km away, provides the energy needed to power all life on Earth.

The International Atomic Energy Association predicts that by 2050 Solar Energy will be the biggest supplier of electricity in the world.

A glimpse of that future can be seen in the development of solar-powered cars by top science, technology and engineering students from universities around the world, including South Africa.

V/O: The ingenuity of some of the very best solar-powered cars ever designed was showcased at the 5th Sasol Solar Challenge.

The event featured 11 teams in an 8-stage trek across South Africa beginning in Pretoria, travelling to waypoints like Kroonstad, Bloemfontein, Port Elizabeth and Swellendam before the finish in Cape Town


Relying solely on the solar power stored in their batteries, the cars travel at an average speed of 100km/hr on South African public roads and can travel up to 200km on a single charge.

John Link: A few days before the race starts, the teams gather at the Zwartkops Raceway, here in Centurion for some important business. All cars have to pass scrutineering tests in order to be allowed to compete. It’s a tense yet exciting affair

Winstone Jordaan: So today’s to look and see: Are they going to be stable on the road, will they be able to break at the right times and do the things we expect.

John Link: Our focus is on some of the South African University teams taking part in the challenge. It’s an opportunity for some of the brightest engineering students in the country to really make their mark and being here at Zwartkops have a conversation with them

INTRO UJ: The University of Johannesburg’s Solar team is 20 strong and we met two of them to chat about their car Illanga

John: It’s a lot more complex than people give you credit for I guess?

Roberto De Carvahlo: A lot of effort and time goes into a car like this and a lot of design and then review, critique, redesign. So yeah, it’s gets really tough and a lot of sleepless nights to get the car ready

John: It’s more than just about crossing the finish line first isn’t it? I mean there’s a lot more involved it seems to me.

Roberto: Primarily it’s to give young engineers training and experience in the practical field and another is to actually research these new and interesting technologies, especially energy where we currently have a major crisis

John: As somebody who is involved so intimately with the vehicle, how stressful is a day like today?

Simo Moroe: It’s stressful, exciting at the same time. We have run into a couple of issues, so as I said the guys are in the garage now working hard. It’s going to be probably another long night and we’re going to keep going. One thing about the team is that we never give up.

INTRO TUT: The Tshwane University of Technology’s entry Sunchaser 2 is a brand new vehicle and their lower budget relative to the other teams makes them underdogs.

Johannes De Vries: It’s about resources, what are your support from industry, what are your support from other universities and how big is your university team? And I think there is quite a big difference if you compare the world champs versus what we’re doing.

John Link: A few moments ago we were reminded about just how dangerous an event like this can be, the North West University’s cSirius got involved in an accident and landed up on its roof. Now this is the car we last saw at the World Solar Challenge but it’s participation in this race is now is jeopardy.

Albert Helberg: We’ve got two choices: leave and just call it quits or just push through and the team spirit is traumatised but they want to carry on.


V/O: After working throughout the night, NWU were able to repair Sirius and take their place amongst the 10 other teams for the start in Pretoria.

To win a team must log the most number of kilometres over the course of the challenge.

The strategy each day is to try cover as much distance as possible without draining the battery with factors such as weather, wind and road incline all affecting performance.

Battery conservation is crucial and if power gets too low, a team must stop to recharge. This can take up 3-5 hours greatly reducing the distance a team is able to log on a stage.

As the challenge unfolded, favourites Nuon from the Netherlands and Tokai from Japan took the lead racking up impressive distances each day

Underdogs Sunchaser 2 more than held their own whilst technical setbacks affected the distance logged by Illanga

Despite their earlier accident, Sirius surpassed expectation. On stage 2 the team logged an impressive 611.9 km, breaking the South African record for the longest distance covered in a single day. By the time they completed the penultimate stage to Swellendam, they were the best placed South African Team in 4th.

LINK: Dawn on the morning of the final stage from Swellendam gave teams the chance to charge their car batteries before the start of the final leg to Cape Town. Having come so far since the start of the challenge, no team wanted to falter at the final hurdle…

Arno De Beer: Yes absolutely fantastic to arrive here today, the final day on our way to Cape Town

Este Hees: No doubt in any of us minds, we are going to see this through and we are still going to be the best South African team and I think thus far, we’ve quite proved it.

Simo Moroe: It’s been a great learning curve. Sure we didn’t finish exactly where we wanted to be but I think all the guys have learnt a lot from this trip when it comes to future cars, we know exactly what to do, what to do differently and how to make better improvements on the car



LINK TO CAPE TOWN: The welcome sight of Table Mountain meant the finish line was just around the corner.

Having overcome the adversity of the accident and despite damage to their solar panels, a triumphant Sirius was in sight of another record: the first South African team to complete the entire distance of the challenge without assistance
John Waterfront Link: So here we are at the V&A Waterfront in Cape Town and the culmination of the 8-day Sasol Solar Challenge. It’s been a race full of ups and downs but ultimately ending in triumph because all of these cars commutatively have done over 25000km all on the power of the sun

V/O: Dutch team Nuon were crowned winners completing 4,716 km and breaking the four-year old record in the process. They beat Japanese team Tokai by 172 km. Hungary’s Megalux came in third with Sirius the top ranked South African team in 4th.

John: So Arno it was touch and go there for you for a while but you made it in the end, you must be absolutely delighted

Arno: We’ve just exceeded our own expectations. We knew our car is good and with a damaged panel we set records.

John: Right now you look absolutely exhausted, how are you feeling?

Simo: This team just wants to keep on learning and keep on growing and that’s what we’ve done with this whole experience.

Johannes: We wanted to have a higher ranking of the South African teams so we’ve aimed for second place of the South African teams and we managed to do that.

OUTRO V/O: As all the teams celebrated their accomplishment of finishing the 5th Sasol Solar Challenge, the spirit of comradery fostered during the race painted a bright future for Solar: a future powered by the energy of the sun, cleaner, greener and renewable.

That said, TUT has one of the best engineering departments in South Africa in terms of research and innovation outputs - and have completely redone their 2016 vehicle from scratch. The shoot will take place over two days: September 22 - Swartkops Raceway: This is a designated track day in which all team cars participating undergo mandatory testing that they have to pass in order to be allowed to compete in the race. All of the teams will be there and I have already secured interviews with team members from NWU, UJ & TUT. We will also have access to their pitlanes to be able to shoot their cars in detail. Whilst at Swartkops, we will also be able to meet some of the international teams taking part including favourites from the Netherlands and Japan September 30 - 1 October - This is the final leg of the race from Swellendam to Cape Town. We will rendezvous with the race at Swellendam on the 30th, camp the night with the teams before they leave at 6:30AM for the final stage to Cape Town. We will shoot this final leg along with the finish at the V&A Waterfront. The 3 SA university teams have agreed to provide R&D material of their cars in the form of video, cad design & still photos to augment the insert. The race organisers have agreed to provide footage of the race (stage 1-7) captured by their videographer
